keyTerms.note: The verb for a matter being decided and finished off. Its passive form here leaves the agent unnamed and makes the point structural: the case is simply never brought to a close.
From the root for lightness. The form implies a load reduced by stages, which is the ordinary human expectation of any hardship, and it is precisely that expectation being denied.
An intensive form from a root covering both the covering over of something and the denial of a favour. The choice ties the outcome to gifts received rather than only to opinions held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In seventh-century Arabia almost every affliction had a horizon. A fever broke, a siege lifted, a debt fell due and was settled, a captive was ransomed by his clan. Even the heaviest penalties a tribe could impose ended, in exile or in death. Listeners had no experience of an unbounded condition, which is why the ayah describes one by removing the two ways out that they knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes this state elsewhere using the same method of denial rather than description. In one passage those inside call out to a keeper asking that their Lord finish them off, and in another a person there is said neither to die nor to live. In each case the language works by closing an exit, not by naming a sensation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places the reckoning outside the arithmetic people normally apply to suffering, in which every pain is measured against its ending. That is uncomfortable by design and the Quran does not soften it here. What it does do is attach the outcome to ingratitude rather than to ignorance, which keeps the surah's whole argument open, since the chapter has spent itself showing gifts to people who can still look at them.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same wish for an ending into the mouths of those inside, and reports the answer they are given.
States the same condition in its shortest form, neither dying there nor living.
Gives the other side of the same root, promising increase to whoever acknowledges what he was given.

studies.applyIt: Take one ordinary thing you used today without noticing: water from a tap, a knee that works, a message from someone who checks on you. Say thanks for that one thing out loud, once. The surah's argument is that ingratitude is not a feeling but a habit of not looking, and the repair for it is correspondingly small and specific.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Life Long Enough
studies.meaning: The request is reasonable and it is refused. Let us out and we will act differently, they say, which concedes the entire argument. The answer does not deny that they would act differently. It asks instead about the time they already had, and phrases the standard not as a fixed number of years but as whether anyone who wanted to take heed could have. Two facts then close the case: the lifespan was granted, and the warner did come. The last clause calls them wrongdoers, not fools.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the description of a punishment that is never lightened. The commentators cite reports about an age past which a person can no longer claim to have been rushed, with sixty years named in more than one of them, and they treat the ayah itself as leaving the term deliberately unspecified. No particular occasion is reported. The surah has already established that a warner reaches every community.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the verb to cry out, carrying an infixed letter that makes the shouting strenuous and sustained. It is a cry for rescue rather than merely a sound of pain.
From the root for lifespan and for inhabiting a place. The verb form means years being granted to someone, which quietly makes the time itself one of the gifts under discussion.
A verb of remembering rather than of learning. It implies the material was already present and needed only attention, which is why the answer given is about time and not about information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Age was social currency in Arabia. Elders arbitrated disputes, and long life was read as accumulated judgement, so a man of sixty who had learned nothing was a recognisable and slightly shameful figure. Genealogies and the memory of abandoned settlements were carried by the oldest men in a camp. The question here, asking what was done with the years, borrows a standard the audience already applied to one another.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for taking heed appears twice inside the same short clause of this ayah, once in a form for ongoing action and once in a form for completed action, so the sentence reads roughly as time in which whoever took heed would take heed. The doubling makes the condition circular on purpose: the years were sufficient for anyone who was going to use them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah answers a question people genuinely ask, whether a second chance would change anything, and declines to answer it on those terms. The issue is not what someone would do with more time but what was done with the time that was theirs. That makes the present moment the entire subject. It also establishes that the reckoning is not about capacity, since the ability to take heed is assumed throughout the sentence.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same request at the moment of death and answers it with a barrier standing until the resurrection.
Reports the same wish to be sent back, and adds that they would return to what they had been forbidden.
Places a version of the plea in the mouth of someone asking for a short delay in order to give in charity.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself in one sentence that begins with when. When work quiets down, when the children are older. Then take the smallest version of that thing which your actual week allows, and do it this week. The ayah is not about laziness. Its whole weight falls on the difference between the time you were given and the time you keep imagining.

studies.title: Knower Of What Chests Hold
studies.meaning: Two claims sit side by side. God knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and He knows what is inside chests, which brings the same knowledge from the largest scale down to the most private one. Then humanity is described as successors placed on the earth, and the consequence of refusal is stated three times over: it falls back on the one refusing, it increases only loathing before his Lord, and it increases only loss. Nothing is added to anyone else's account.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just reported the plea from the Fire and the answer given to it, and now steps back to the two facts that make such a reckoning possible: complete knowledge, and a delegated position on earth that can be misused. The commentators report no occasion. The word for successors picks up the argument the surah keeps making about earlier communities that held the land and are gone.

keyTerms.note: What is absent from perception rather than what is mysterious. The root is used of a man away on a journey, so the word covers what is merely out of view as much as what is unknowable.
An idiom for the contents of a person's inner life. The construction names the very substance of the chests rather than only their secrets, which is why translators reach for what hearts hide.
A plural for people who take the place of others. It carries a position of authority and, at the same time, the plain fact of replacement, since every successor stands where someone else once stood.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia was full of the traces of people who had been replaced. Dry wells, abandoned terraces in the south, rock inscriptions in a script nobody in Mecca could read. Caravans passed the remains of settlements whose names survived only in poetry. That a people holds a place for a while and then hands it on was not theology to that audience. It was scenery along a trade route.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as what chests contain occurs in twelve ayat of the Quran, and in every one of them it is attached to God's knowledge and to no one else's. Here it arrives immediately after a scene in which people are speaking and pleading, so the two ways of knowing a person, by what is said and by what is held, are placed back to back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting the unseen of the universe and the contents of a chest inside one sentence collapses the distance between them. A person can be hidden from every other observer and is not hidden at all. The second ayah then makes refusal entirely self-contained: it damages nothing above and nothing outside, only the one holding it. That removes both the fear that unbelief injures God and the idea that it is a neutral private matter.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same clause about what chests contain, at the end of a warning about concealed hostility.
Uses the same word for successors on the earth and adds that differing ranks among them are part of the test.
Makes the same two points, that disbelief cannot reach God and no one carries another's load, ending on knowledge of chests.

studies.applyIt: Choose one thing you are carrying that nobody around you knows about, and do not tell anyone. Sit with it for a minute while holding the fact that it is already fully known. Most people find this cuts both ways at once, exposure and relief. Notice which of the two you feel more, because it tells you something about what you are carrying.

studies.title: Show Me What They Created
studies.meaning: The challenge is put as an audit. Show me what your partners made of the earth. Do they own any share in the heavens. Was a book given, so that you are standing on something clear from it. Three possible grounds for a religious claim, in descending order of ambition, and the passage does not wait for an answer before drawing its conclusion. What is left is people making promises to each other, and the word for what they promise means a pleasing deception rather than an honest mistake.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a city whose religious life and much of whose income were organised around a sanctuary crowded with idols. The commentators report no specific occasion. The argument runs on ground the audience already accepted, since the Meccans did not claim their deities had created anything and generally described them as intermediaries. Asking for creation, ownership or a scripture was asking for something they knew they could not produce.

keyTerms.note: An imperative for producing something to be looked at, not for explaining it. The demand is for evidence a person could point to, which is why the three questions after it concern ownership or a document.
The ordinary commercial word for a stake in a joint venture. Using it turns a theological claim into a question about title, and the same root gives the word for associating partners with God.
From a root about being taken in by something attractive. It names a deception the victim enjoys, which is why the same word is used elsewhere of the life of this world itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan commerce ran on shares. Men bought fractions of a caravan's cargo, and disputes were settled by asking who had put in what. A claim to a share that could not be evidenced was a familiar kind of fraud, and the vocabulary for testing it was everyday speech in the city. The ayah asks exactly the question a merchant would put to a partner who wanted a payout.
studies.didYouKnow: A passage in another surah runs this same challenge in almost the same words, asking to be shown what was created of the earth and whether there is any share in the heavens, and then adds a further demand for a scripture from before this one or a remnant of knowledge. Reading the two together shows the argument being made in a fixed form rather than improvised.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah defines the ground on which a religious claim can stand: having made something, having a share in something, or having been given a document. Nothing else is listed, and inherited practice is not on the list. That standard cuts in both directions, which is why the surah elsewhere rests its own claim on a book confirming earlier books. The closing line then locates the real engine of false devotion in mutual assurance between people.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same demand in nearly identical wording and adds a request for an earlier scripture or a trace of knowledge.
Puts the challenge as a display: this is God's creation, now show me what those besides Him have made.
Reduces the same demand to its smallest possible form, asking whether they could between them create a fly.

studies.applyIt: Take one position you hold strongly and ask which of the three grounds it stands on: something you built, something you have a stake in, or something you were shown in writing. If the honest answer is that people around you also hold it, that is not a reason to drop it. It is a reason to go and find the actual ground before you defend it again.

studies.title: He Holds Them From Falling
studies.meaning: The heavens and the earth are described as things that would go if they were not held. The verb is the one this surah used in its second ayah for a mercy nobody can withhold, so the chapter states its argument twice with the same image of a grip. The conditional then makes the point unanswerable: were they to give way, no one after Him could hold them. The two names at the end are the surprise, since forbearing and forgiving belong to the language of dealing with people.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the challenge to the idols to show what they created or what they own. Having asked what the partners made, the ayah states who is currently keeping everything in place. No occasion is reported. The commentators connect the closing names to the holding itself: a world that continues while its inhabitants deny its Maker is presented as an instance of restraint rather than of indifference.

keyTerms.note: A verb of grip and restraint, used of holding water in a vessel or a hand on a rope. The same root opens this surah, where nothing can hold back a mercy God releases.
A dual verb for shifting out of place and ceasing. Arabic marks pairs grammatically, so the sentence treats sky and earth as one structure that would go together or not at all.
Restraint in someone with the power to act now. It is not mildness of temperament but a deliberate delay, which is why it stands beside forgiving at the end of an ayah about holding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Building in Arabia was mostly a matter of things staying up under their own weight: dry stone, mud brick, a tent held by the tension between pegs and poles. Everyone had watched a wall go and knew a structure is only as good as whatever resists the pull on it. A sky and an earth requiring continuous holding was not abstract physics to that audience but the daily condition of every shelter they made.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the verb for holding occurs in only two ayat of this surah, the second one and this one, four ayat from the end. In the first, nothing can hold back a mercy God releases or release what He holds. In the second, nothing but He holds the heavens and the earth. The chapter is framed by the same grip at both ends.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Existence is presented as a continuous act rather than a completed one. Nothing here runs on inherited momentum, which makes the ordinary persistence of the world an event and not a default setting. The two closing names then extend that same grip into the moral order. What is being held back is not only collapse but consequence, and the ayah puts the two restraints in one sentence without explaining how they are connected.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for holding the sky back from falling on the earth except by His permission.
Describes the heaven and the earth standing by His command, then a single call that raises the dead.
Adds a further detail, a sky raised without any pillars that can be seen, holding the same idea differently.

studies.applyIt: Look at something in your life that is currently holding: a marriage, a job, your health, a friendship that survived a bad year. You did not check on it this morning because it has been steady. Spend one minute treating that steadiness as something being done rather than something that is simply the case, and thank the one doing it.

studies.title: The Oath They Did Not Keep
studies.meaning: They swore by God, using the strongest oath formula their language had, that a warner reaching them would find them better guided than any earlier community. The oath appears to have been meant when it was made, which is what gives the ayah its sting. When the warner actually arrived, the only measurable change was that they moved further away. The commentators read the oath as a comparison with scriptural communities the Arabs knew had fallen short, and the ayah as showing that hypothetical piety is not piety.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Arabs of the region knew the scriptural communities north and south of them and were aware of their internal criticisms, and the commentators report that some in Mecca did say they would do better if a book came in their own language. When it came, most of the city refused it. The surah has already established that a warner passes through every community, so the excuse of never having been told was closed in advance.

keyTerms.note: Literally the utmost of their oaths, an idiom for the strongest formula available. It marks not merely swearing but straining the language of swearing as far as that language will go.
A construction leaving the comparison open rather than naming a rival. The claim is to outdo whichever community you care to pick, which is exactly the shape of a boast that costs nothing.
The word used of an animal shying and running from something. It describes a reflex rather than a considered rejection, which is why the ayah presents it as an increase and not a decision.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were the load-bearing structure of Arabian society. With no courts to enforce contracts, a sworn word secured caravan shares, protection agreements and blood settlements, and a broken oath damaged a whole clan's standing. Swearing by God with the strongest formula was the most expensive thing a man could spend. What the ayah describes is worse than a lie: a promise made in the most serious currency available, then abandoned when it became real.
studies.didYouKnow: The idiom for the strongest oaths occurs in five ayat of the Quran, and in each of them the oath is one the passage goes on to treat as unreliable, whether it promises belief, obedience or a denial of the resurrection. The Arabic phrase means something closer to the exertion of their oaths, as though the swearing itself were physical labour.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line between imagined faith and the actual kind. What a person would do under better conditions is not evidence about them, because the conditions they would have to act in are the ones they already have. It also shows that a demand met can harden rather than convince, which reframes the whole question of the miracles the Meccans kept requesting. The arrival of what was asked for produced flight.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same oath formula for a promise to believe if a sign came, and questions whether it would be kept.
Records the excuse this oath was built on, that a scripture given to us would have found us better guided.
Shows the same strongest oaths spent instead on denying outright that God will raise the dead.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself in one sentence that begins if I had. If I had more time I would visit them. If I had money I would give properly. Then take the smallest version of that thing your actual circumstances allow and do it this week. The ayah is not about lying. It is about what happens to a promise on the day its condition finally arrives.

studies.title: Scheming Closes On Its Authors
studies.meaning: The aversion of the previous ayah is given two causes: acting greater than one is, and the plotting of evil. Then a rule is stated about how plotting behaves. Evil scheming closes in on nobody except the people who made it. The Arabic verb is one of encirclement, so the plot is pictured surrounding its own authors rather than being punished from outside. The passage ends by naming God's settled practice with earlier peoples and saying twice that it admits neither substitution nor diversion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators connect the plotting here with the planning against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in Mecca, without tying the ayah to one incident. The surah has just described an oath abandoned the moment its condition arrived. The reference to the practice of the ancients points the audience toward the ruined communities along their own trade routes, whose fate the chapter treats as documented rather than legendary.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to seek or claim greatness rather than to possess it. The grammar makes arrogance a performance a person keeps up, which is why the ayah pairs it immediately with scheming.
A verb for something encircling and then coming down on what it surrounds. In the Quran its subject is regularly the very thing people made light of, catching up with them later.
A course followed consistently enough to become predictable, from a root about a path worn smooth by use. Applied to God, it names regularity in the way communities are dealt with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal politics ran on manoeuvre. Alliances were made to isolate a rival clan, boycotts were organised, marriages arranged to shift a balance of power. Everyone in Mecca understood plotting as a legitimate instrument and expected to be plotted against in turn. What the ayah adds is not a warning about getting caught but a claim about the shape of the thing: the trap is built by people standing inside it.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah closes with two different nouns for change, one meaning substitution and the other meaning diversion, and it is the only place in the Quran where both appear together. The first occurs in four other ayat and the second in two, so the denial made once elsewhere is deliberately doubled here at the end of a warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Moral consequence is described as a structural feature rather than an intervention. A plot does not need to be punished from outside, because it returns to its authors through the way it was built. That is then generalised into a claim about God's dealings being consistent, which cuts both ways. It removes the hope of an exception, and it equally removes the fear of arbitrariness, since a practice that cannot be diverted is one that can be relied upon.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle from the other side, that schemers plot against themselves without perceiving it.
Names the same unchanging practice of God, using one of the two words for change that appear here.
Narrates the rule as a story: a plot laid carefully, and the outcome landing on the ones who laid it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you arranged something to come out in your favour without anyone noticing the arrangement. Not a crime, just a manoeuvre. Ask what it cost you internally to keep it running. That cost is the ayah's point. Today, choose the direct version of one small thing you were about to handle indirectly.

studies.title: Travel And Look At Endings
studies.meaning: The instruction is to go and look. Not to reason about history but to move through land where the evidence is still standing, and to observe how things finished for the people who were there before. The comparison is made in one clause: they were stronger. That closes off the escape of assuming those civilisations fell because they were weak. The ayah then denies that anything in the heavens or the earth can reduce God to incapacity, and ends on two names, knowing and powerful.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Meccans were traders whose routes ran north past settlements carved into rock and abandoned, and south toward the remains of the old kingdoms of Arabia with their broken irrigation works. No occasion is reported for the ayah. Its instruction is unusually concrete for a surah that has argued mostly from nature, and it works because the audience genuinely made these journeys twice a year.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for journeying, not for pilgrimage or campaign. It asks for the trips the audience already made rather than for anything additional, which is what makes the question pointed.
From the root for a heel and for what follows behind. It names the outcome that arrives last, so the word carries a sense of the ending being attached to everything that preceded it.
A verb about reducing someone to incapacity, from the root for weakness. The denial is precise: no thing anywhere diminishes His capacity, which is why the ayah closes on power.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Meccan trade year had two great journeys, one north toward Syria in summer and one south toward the Yemen in winter. Both passed physical remains: facades cut into cliffs with nobody living behind them, and in the south the memory of a great dam and the terraced land it had watered. Caravan men told stories about these places at halts. The ayah asks them to treat the scenery as evidence.
studies.didYouKnow: The question about travelling in the land and looking occurs in seven ayat of the Quran, spread across surahs from very different periods, and in six of the seven what is to be looked at is named as the outcome rather than the ruin. It is one of the Book's few instructions to go and verify something physically instead of reflecting on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faith is asked here to rest partly on observation. The passage offers no private intuition and no miracle but a public record anyone can walk through, and it forbids the comfortable explanation that those peoples fell for want of strength. Then it names why strength is no help: incapacity cannot be inflicted on God by anything at all. Knowledge and power are given as a pair, so the outcome is neither accident nor arbitrary blow.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the instruction and adds that the earlier peoples worked the land more thoroughly than these ones did.
Asks the same question and notes that what those people had gained availed them nothing in the end.
Supplies one worked example, a southern kingdom with gardens and a dam, and what came after it.

studies.applyIt: Next time you pass an old building coming down or a shop that has closed after years of trading, stop for ten seconds instead of walking on. Ask what ended, and when it started ending. The ayah's method is not moralising about ruins. It is the ordinary discipline of letting something finished tell you about something still running.

studies.title: Not A Creature Would Remain
studies.meaning: The surah ends on a conditional that never becomes real. If God took people to account for what they have earned, nothing that moves on the earth would be left. The commentators note the reach of the statement, since it takes in every living creature and not only the wrongdoers. What happens instead is a delay to a named term. The chapter then closes not with a threat but with sight: when that term arrives, God is one who sees His servants.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the final ayah of the surah. The chapter has moved through creation, provision, the two outcomes, the plea from the Fire and the ruins of earlier peoples, and it ends by explaining why the world is still standing. No occasion is reported. For an audience being told repeatedly about communities that were destroyed, the last word is that the delay they are living inside is itself the answer.

keyTerms.note: Anything that walks or crawls on the earth, from a verb about moving slowly along the ground. It is the widest available word for living things, which is what makes the conditional so sweeping.
A fixed period whose end has been specified. The passive participle matters: the term is not merely fixed but named by someone, so the delay is a decision rather than an indefinite drift.
Sight rather than mere knowledge, which in Arabic usage implies attention turned toward a particular thing. Ending the surah on this name leaves the reckoning personal instead of statistical.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Mecca ran on named terms. A loan was extended to a fixed date, often the return of a caravan, and everyone understood the difference between a debt forgiven and a debt deferred. Traders lived inside such deferrals for months at a stretch and never mistook one for the other. The ayah uses that exact structure, and its first audience knew precisely which kind of relief was being described.
studies.didYouKnow: Almost this same sentence appears in one other surah, with one difference: there the reason given is their wrongdoing, and here it is what they have earned. That other version adds that when the term comes they will not delay it by an hour, while this one ends instead on God seeing His servants, so the two close on judgement and on attention.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage explains the continued existence of the world as an active restraint rather than as evidence that nothing is being counted. That reframes patience, since the delay a person experiences as silence is described here as a decision with a date attached to it. And by widening the conditional to every moving creature, it makes human conduct something that reaches past the person, which is a claim about consequence rather than a rule about behaviour.

studies.applyIt: Think about something you got away with. Not the dramatic kind, the ordinary kind: the unkindness nobody called you on, the corner quietly cut. Instead of relief, treat the silence that followed as room you were given. Use ten minutes of that room today to repair one specific thing, while repairing it is still cheap and still available.
